title: The Two Economies of AI: When Compute Is Free and When It Isn't

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: Welcome back, everyone! Today we're diving into a radical shift in how we think about AI compute—what the CommandCenter team calls the Two Economies Doctrine.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Exactly. Most AI systems are built on one assumption: every token costs money. That shapes everything—from prompt length to agent behavior. But the Two Economies Doctrine flips that on its head.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So there’s not just one kind of compute? There are two?

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Yes. First, there’s sunk compute—the hardware you’ve already paid for. Like OMEN’s two Intel Arc Pro B70s, or the older RTX 2070 Super. You bought them. The cost is in the past. The only real marginal cost is electricity—pennies per hour.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So if I’m running a model on that hardware, the cost per token is basically zero?

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Effectively, yes. That’s why we call it the sunk economy. You can run twenty variations of a prompt, generate a 12,000-token draft, throw it away, and try again—all without blinking. The cost isn’t in the tokens, it’s in the kilowatt-hour.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: That sounds like a dream. So what’s the other economy? The one where tokens still cost money?

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: The metered frontier. Think Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro—models so large they can’t run locally. Every token here is billed. They have rate limits, latency, and budgets. You can’t just fire them off like a local script.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So if I use a frontier model to reformat JSON, I’m basically hiring a Supreme Court Justice to stamp parking tickets?

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Exactly. That’s the core discipline of the Two Economies Doctrine: keep them strictly separated. Sunk compute is the factory floor—doing drafting, linting, background checks. Frontier compute is the appellate court—handling high-level architecture, trade-off decisions, and arbitration.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So how do you actually enforce that boundary in practice?

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Through configuration. In `operations.toml`, each operation has ceilings—max prompt size, token limits, and deadlines. In `backends.toml`, backends declare their cost class. Local runners like `omen-arc` have no cost class. Cloud ones like `gcp-gemini` are marked `trial`, with a global cap of 200 million tokens and a hard stop at 20 million.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: And the scheduler figures out which one to use?

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Yes. When a build worker dispatches a task, the scheduler checks the runner class. Local tasks go to the B70s or FX99. Frontier tasks are metered, audited, and logged like financial transactions.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So what does true autonomous engineering actually look like under this model?

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: It’s not about having a better model. It’s about making the cost of trying an idea drop to zero. When you don’t fear the bill, an agent can test three different architectures overnight, run them against a live harness, discard the weak ones, and have a winning PR ready by morning coffee.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So the real breakthrough isn’t in the model—it’s in the economics.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Precisely. Hearth isn’t just routing API calls. It’s defending the boundary between infinite local experiment and surgical cloud intelligence. That’s where autonomy really lives.
